{{Short description|Sequence of integers}}
The '''Pillai sequence''' is the [[integer sequence|sequence of integers]] that have record numbers of terms in their greedy representations as sums of [[prime number]]s (and one). It is named after [[Subbayya Sivasankaranarayana Pillai]], who first defined it in 1930.<ref>{{citation|first=S. S.|last=Pillai|title=An arithmetical function concerning primes|journal=Annamalai University Journal|year=1930|pages=159–167}}. As cited by {{harvtxt|Luca|Thangadurai|2009}}.</ref>

It would follow from [[Goldbach's conjecture]] that every integer greater than one can be represented as a sum of at most three [[prime number]]s. However, finding such a representation could involve solving instances of the [[subset sum problem]], which is computationally difficult. Instead, Pillai considered the following simpler [[greedy algorithm]] for finding a representation of <math>n</math> as a sum of primes: choose the first prime in the sum to be the largest prime <math>p</math> that is at most <math>n</math>, and then recursively construct the remaining sum recursively for <math>n-p</math>. If this process reaches zero, then it halts; if it reaches one instead of zero, then it must include one in the sum (even though it is not prime), and then halt. For instance, this algorithm represents 122 as 113 + 7 + 2, even though the shorter representations 61 + 61 or 109 + 13 are also possible.

The <math>n</math>th number in the Pillai sequence is the smallest number whose greedy representation as a sum of primes (and one) requires <math>n</math> terms. These numbers are
:0, 1, 4, 27, 1354, 401429925999155061, ... {{OEIS|A066352}}.
Each number <math>a(n)</math> in the sequence is the sum of the previous number <math>a(n-1)</math> with a prime number <math>p</math>, the smallest prime whose following [[prime gap]] is larger than <math>a(n-1)</math>.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Luca | first1 = Florian | author1-link = Florian Luca
 | last2 = Thangadurai | first2 = Ravindranathan
 | issue = 3
 | journal = Journal de Théorie des Nombres de Bordeaux
 | mr = 2605540
 | pages = 693–699
 | title = On an arithmetic function considered by Pillai
 | url = https://jtnb.cedram.org/item?id=JTNB_2009__21_3_693_0
 | volume = 21
 | year = 2009| doi = 10.5802/jtnb.695 | doi-access = free
 }}</ref> For instance, the number 27 in the sequence is 4 + 23, and the first prime gap larger than 4 is the one between 23 and 29.

Because the prime numbers become less dense as they become larger (as quantified by the [[prime number theorem]]), there is always a prime gap larger than any term in the Pillai sequence, so the sequence continues to an infinite number of terms. However, the terms in the sequence grow very rapidly; [[Cramér's conjecture]] implies the sequence grows [[tetration]]ally.<ref name="oeis" /> It has been estimated that expressing the next term in the sequence would require "hundreds of millions of digits".<ref name="oeis">{{Cite OEIS|A066352|name=Pillai sequence|mode=cs2}}</ref>
